key_finding: A field-experiment nudge that discourages minimum-only credit-card payments cut minimum-only paying by 23% at six months but did not significantly reduce debt, because nudged cardholders mostly chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and liquidity-constrained cardholders were disproportionately affected.
methodology: Field experiment with credit card issuer, six-month follow-up on payment and debt outcomes; abstract gives effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's objection in a real consumer financial product: a nudge changed a nominal enrollment-like metric while leaving the real outcome (debt/savings) unmoved, and hurt liquidity-constrained users most \u2014 exactly the enrollment-vs-amount and distributional questions the brief asks about.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not a savings product
six-month horizon only
US regulatory context, not EU
relevance_reason: Consumer financial product field RCT showing enrollment-metric change without real behavioral change, with a liquidity-driven distributional finding.

key_finding: A narrative overview of DC plan design summarizing how automatic enrollment and default investment choices affect participation, contribution rates and engagement, including negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative literature overview, no new empirical estimates; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Useful high-level orientation on the employer-retirement literature the brief explicitly says is the closest analogy but whose intermediary mechanism does not transfer; not itself decision-changing for the round-up feature.
limitations: employer-sponsored DC retirement plans, not a consumer app
no effect sizes given
not a systematic review
relevance_reason: Broad review of the adjacent employer-retirement default literature, useful background but off the brief's setting.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises retirement plan participation but tends to induce passivity \u2014 low contribution anchoring, inactive account management, and account churn \u2014 such that participation gains alone do not demonstrate welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative synthesis of default-enrollment literature with policy recommendations; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: States the core passivity-and-vanity-metric concern the support team raises, but in employer retirement terms with no new data; a weaker, lower-citation restatement of stronger papers in this set.
limitations: US employer retirement setting
no citation/effect-size evidence given
zero citations, unestablished venue
relevance_reason: Directly frames the enrollment-vs-engagement tension the brief cares about, though as commentary rather than new evidence.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when and how default choice architecture produces downstream (persistent) effects on consumer behavior, identifying time course, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical synthesis of the consumer-defaults literature building a research agenda; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the project a framework for exactly the question it needs answered \u2014 whether the round-up default will persist or fade \u2014 by naming the conditions (salience, antecedent preference strength) under which defaults do or don't stick, which should shape what to measure post-launch.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical, not a new empirical estimate
no specific effect sizes
not focused on financial products specifically
relevance_reason: The clearest general-consumer (non-employer) synthesis of when default effects persist versus decay, directly informing the persistence question.

key_finding: Default plan assignment in Medicare Part D has large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option, even when it causes substantial welfare losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a large administrative dataset of low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Strong causal evidence that default effects persist and that passivity is not simply a signal of 'the default is fine' \u2014 relevant to whether an opt-out round-up default would similarly capture inattentive users regardless of fit, informing distributional risk.
limitations: health-insurance/drug-plan setting, not a financial product
government/administrative default rather than a fintech app
no employer, but also no financial-savings context
relevance_reason: Rigorous evidence on persistence and insensitivity of passive default-following in a non-employer, individual-choice setting, useful analogy though off the financial domain.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default savings-rate auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of those defaulted into escalation actually escalate on the first date.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, vesting, withdrawal-on-separation, and opt-out from auto-escalation.
why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrollment lift is real at signup and much smaller once job turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out are accounted for, meaning enrollment numbers can be a vanity metric relative to actual amounts saved.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated setting
US 401(k) institutional specifics may not map onto app defaults
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving once medium/long-run attrition is accounted for, which the brief explicitly asked us to look for.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees into a public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opted out, with the default effect strongest when incentives are higher and knowledge of enrollment status is lower.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around the nationwide auto-enrollment policy introduction.
why_it_matters: A large, precise recent effect size for opt-out enrollment moderated by incentive salience and awareness \u2014 useful benchmark for how big an enrollment lift to expect, but in a public pension context.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension, not a consumer fintech product
government rather than employer-or-app intermediary
no medium-term amount-saved outcome given
relevance_reason: Recent natural experiment quantifying the default effect size and its moderators, relevant by analogy to the enrollment decision.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, confirmed at 12 months across over 100 US plans and a UK panel, attenuate substantially by 36 months, with only modest average savings increases though a significant reduction in savings inequality.
methodology: Empirical analysis of >100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a calibrated life-cycle consumption-savings model (switching cost ~$250).
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the persistence question the brief asks about \u2014 defaults raise enrollment sharply at signup but the effect decays by medium-run horizons \u2014 and shows a distributional upside (reduced inequality) even as average gains shrink.
limitations: employer/occupational retirement plans, not a consumer app
US/UK pension systems, not EU liquid savings
life-cycle model calibration adds structural assumptions
relevance_reason: Strong recent multi-horizon evidence on default-effect attenuation and distributional impact, the kind of medium-run persistence data the brief needs, though in an employer pension setting.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges on risk-taking have medium-to-large effects, but implementing a default nudge \u2014 and especially having individuals refuse it \u2014 lowers users' rating of the advice/advisor, and framing of the default presentation shifts chosen allocations.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country EU sample, manipulating default presence and framing of a financial-allocation decision.
why_it_matters: Gives EU-context evidence that a financial default can be perceived as manipulative and damage trust when refused, directly bearing on the dark-pattern/reputational risk question, and shows framing of the default choice anchors the amount chosen \u2014 relevant to how to phrase the multiplier default.
limitations: risk-allocation/investment decision rather than round-up savings specifically
wealth-manager advice framing, not a self-serve app flow
effect on trust measured via ratings, not actual complaints or churn
relevance_reason: Recent EU-sample experimental evidence directly on when a financial default reads as manipulative versus helpful, and on framing-driven anchoring \u2014 exactly the manipulation-risk and anchoring questions in the brief.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking participation, contribution rates and fund choice under automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset default level anchors the contribution rate people end up at for years, which is the closest classic precedent for our worry that a preset multiplier will anchor users at a suboptimal level \u2014 but it is the older pension literature the brief says is superseded by newer, non-employer work.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), the exact setting the brief says doesn't transfer
no publication year given
predates the app/EU regulatory context the brief cares about
relevance_reason: Classic foundational anchoring-on-default-level result that later, more relevant work responds to.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million tipping decisions shows default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost (84% of adherence needs both), and adding a lower preset option (15%) below an existing 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at low revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey; counterfactual menu-design simulation.
why_it_matters: The specific technique here \u2014 decomposing why a preset menu of options anchors choices, and simulating how adding/removing a preset level changes both the chosen level and welfare \u2014 is exactly the analysis needed to decide whether to ship a 1x/2x/5x multiplier menu and which value to pre-select.
limitations: setting is tip percentages on taxi rides, not savings contributions
no persistence/withdrawal outcomes measured
welfare framework is revenue-focused, not consumer-protection focused
relevance_reason: Method directly transferable to the multiplier-menu design decision: structural decomposition of why a preset level anchors choice and how changing the menu shifts outcomes.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term, withdraw-anytime savings account offered via payroll deduction at five UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate an account, but among those who did, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of a choice-architecture intervention at five UK firms tracking account activation and 12-month usage among an opt-in short-term savings product.
why_it_matters: The closest existing empirical analog to the round-up pot itself \u2014 a liquid, withdraw-anytime savings product under opt-in \u2014 giving real numbers on the opt-in take-up/engagement trade-off: very low uptake but strong persistence and continued contribution among those who join, directly informing what to expect from an opt-in design.
limitations: enrollment channel is payroll deduction at an employer, not a standalone app
UK firms only, five-firm sample
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice arms in this specific study
relevance_reason: Same liquid short-term savings product structure as the round-up feature, giving direct opt-in take-up and 12-month persistence numbers rather than a retirement-plan analogy.

key_finding: Derives a general characterization of optimal default options via asymptotic approximations, showing that when designer and chooser agree on the activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions to cases of disagreement and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Theoretical mechanism-design model with asymptotic analysis and numerical simulation; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative framework for choosing which multiplier level to pre-select and how much weight to put on minimizing opt-outs versus welfare, but it is abstract theory with no product-specific calibration.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical application to any financial product
asymptotic approximations may not hold well away from limiting cases
no discussion of manipulation perception or regulatory framing
relevance_reason: General theoretical framework for optimal default design, relevant to the preset-level decision though not empirically grounded in a consumer financial setting.

key_finding: Maps EU law on dark patterns to a taxonomy of six autonomy-violation categories, framing regulation as protection of consumer autonomy rather than a blanket ban on defaults.
methodology: Legal doctrinal analysis and taxonomy-building across EU consumer-protection law; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the actual EU legal test for when a default or pre-selection crosses from helpful into a sanctionable dark pattern, which is exactly the reputational-risk question the opt-out design raises.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence on enrolment or amounts
no direct evidence on savings-app behaviour
relevance_reason: Provides the EU regulatory framework for judging whether an opt-out round-up default would read as manipulative, directly bearing on the entry-design decision.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees remained at the default 12 months after hire (vs. ~50% at lower defaults), and remaining defaulters had systematically lower income, showing the default anchors a suboptimal contribution level.
methodology: Analysis of administrative retirement-plan data plus a literature review of default retention rates; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the anchoring risk the brief asks about — a high pre-set level can trap low-income users at a suboptimal amount rather than the level they'd have actively chosen.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
no employer-intermediary comparison to a self-directed setting
relevance_reason: Best available quantitative evidence on whether a pre-set default level anchors people below what they'd otherwise choose.

key_finding: Title indicates field experiments on automating short-term payroll savings in the UK, but the abstract text is not usable.
methodology: abstract-only (text missing/corrupted); described as four large UK field experiments.
why_it_matters: Could bear on short-term, liquid automatic-savings design by the same research team behind other automatic-enrolment work, but no usable content is available to judge this.
limitations: abstract text is essentially unreadable ('Trant')
unclear whether this concerns payroll (employer-mediated) or a genuinely consumer-directed product
relevance_reason: Topically adjacent (short-term automatic savings) but currently unusable as evidence due to missing abstract content.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrolment into just-in-time overdraft alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17–19% and arranged charges 4–8%, worth £170–240 million market-wide, though users still capture less than half of available savings.
methodology: Large-scale field experiments at major UK banks testing automatic enrolment into SMS alerts.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world analogue to our feature: a consumer bank testing automatic enrolment into a low-friction financial nudge at scale, with real behavioural and monetary effect sizes — sets the benchmark our own default-effect measurement should be compared against.
limitations: studies alerts, not a savings/contribution feature per se
no explicit 6–12 month persistence analysis reported
relevance_reason: Directly relevant, same-sector (UK banking), automatic-enrolment field evidence with quantified financial outcomes.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrolment raises savings (£32–38/month) but is partially offset by increased unsecured debt (£7/month) and higher mortgage uptake over 41 months, though defaults also modestly improve credit scores and reduce defaults.
methodology: Randomized policy roll-out of UK automatic-enrolment pensions to ~160,000 small employers, tracked over 41 months.
why_it_matters: Shows that a default can raise nominal savings while triggering offsetting financial behaviour — the kind of unintended consequence the brief wants surfaced before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: employer-sponsored pension, not a self-directed consumer product
debt and mortgage outcomes may not map onto liquid round-up savings
relevance_reason: Strong evidence that default-driven savings increases can be partly illusory once offsetting debt behaviour is accounted for.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrolment 'ordeal' (extra step) to a health-insurance auto-enrolment policy cut enrolment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and disadvantaged people, undermining the rationale that friction selectively screens out low-value enrollees.
methodology: Natural policy experiment analyzing removal of an auto-enrolment default in a public health-insurance program, with a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Warns that adding friction (an active-choice-like step) to remove a default can disproportionately harm the least advantaged rather than screening for genuine disinterest — a distributional risk to weigh against 'active choice' as a supposedly neutral middle option.
limitations: public health-insurance selection market, not a consumer savings product
friction here is an 'ordeal', not exactly an active-choice screen
relevance_reason: Directly evidences distributional harm from removing a default, relevant to who is helped/hurt by design choice.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign sites raised donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on small, first-time donors who likely did not intend the recurring commitment.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across multiple 2020 U.S. campaign websites exploiting different rollout timing of pre-checked recurring-donation boxes.
why_it_matters: Gives a real quantified case of a recurring-contribution default producing unintended enrolment and elevated 'refunds' (a direct analogue to complaints/withdrawals) concentrated among naive users — precisely the support team's worry, with dollar figures attached.
limitations: political donations, not a banking savings product
no 6–12 month persistence tracking beyond refund requests
relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative case of a recurring-contribution default causing disproportionate harm to inexperienced, small-scale users.

key_finding: A default option raises the reservation utility for search (a reference effect) and induces self-selection, so those who reject the default and search further tend to find better options than the default.
methodology: Theoretical search model with reference-dependent utility, tested in a laboratory experiment.
why_it_matters: Offers a mechanism for why anchoring on a preset level could still let motivated users find a better option, informing how much weight to give anchoring concerns for the multiplier decision.
limitations: general lab search task, not a financial product setting
abstract gives no concrete effect sizes
relevance_reason: Provides a theoretical/experimental account of default anchoring and self-selection relevant to whether the preset multiplier would trap users below their true preference.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with the effect persisting at least 15 months post-rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered EU DMA choice-screen mandate on iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: The most directly comparable EU evidence on whether an active-choice screen can substantially shift behaviour away from an incumbent default, with the effect measured well past initial rollout — central to the active-choice-vs-default decision.
limitations: studies browser choice, not financial contribution decisions
cross-platform differences (iOS vs Android rollout) complicate a single effect-size estimate
relevance_reason: Best available recent EU evidence quantifying an active-choice mandate's effect on real behaviour, with persistence beyond a year.

key_finding: A usability study (n=410) of nine opt-out privacy-choice interface designs found that generalizable schemes reduced disruption substantially (98% of participants felt unaffected for the least-disruptive scheme, a 40-point improvement) at a small cost to opt-out utility.
methodology: Browser-extension implementation of nine Global Privacy Control opt-out schemes tested in a usability study with 410 participants.
why_it_matters: Offers concrete interface-design lessons for making an active-choice (no-default) flow low-friction and non-disruptive, useful if legal or reputational concerns push toward active choice over defaults.
limitations: privacy opt-out context, not a financial savings decision
no measure of downstream enrolment or savings behaviour
relevance_reason: Provides usability evidence for designing a low-disruption forced-choice screen, relevant if active choice is selected as the entry design.

key_finding: Opt-out defaults for exam sign-up raised nominal sign-up in field experiments, but only raised actual effortful completion (exam participation and passing) among students who had a prior history of being responsive to university communication; non-responsive students showed higher sign-up with no gain in the target outcome.
methodology: Field experiments changing university exam sign-up to opt-out for one exam and for many exams, with heterogeneity analysis by prior responsiveness.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the support team's exact worry in an effortful-task setting: a default can inflate nominal participation while leaving real engagement unchanged for a large, identifiable subgroup, suggesting who a round-up default would and would not help.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial product
effortful task requiring 'responsiveness' may not map directly onto passive automatic savings
relevance_reason: Closest evidence that a default can raise enrolment numbers without changing effortful/engaged outcomes, mirroring the brief's core enrolment-vs-engagement worry.

key_finding: After target-date funds became the default retirement-plan investment option post-2006 pension reform, workers' equity allocation became age-dependent, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level analysis of millions of U.S. retirement investors, 2006–2018, around the Pension Protection Act.
why_it_matters: Suggests defaults can reshape a downstream choice (asset allocation) while leaving the upstream contribution-rate decision largely untouched, a mild data point on whether presets change amounts or only nominal parameters, but at some remove from our decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement investment, not a consumer app or contribution-level decision
focuses on portfolio composition, not enrolment or contribution rate anchoring directly
relevance_reason: Background evidence on defaults affecting one behaviour but not another, of limited direct use to the round-up design decisions.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges, and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise the brief asks us to test, with an RCT rather than an anecdote, and shows the effect can reverse depending on cultural/institutional trust — exactly the kind of evidence needed before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: hypothetical/survey-based willingness rather than real enrolment behaviour
Chinese voluntary-pension context, not an EU consumer savings app
small sample (n=220)
relevance_reason: The clearest counter-evidence in this batch that a default can reduce rather than raise savings intentions, fulfilling the brief's explicit call for a contradicting study.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people generally approve of financial 'nudges,' with strong preferences for System 2 (deliberative) interventions and savings-framed interventions, and approval did not depend on transparency or on whether a bank was the messenger.
methodology: Pre-registered vignette survey with 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios, varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting; representative Australian sample, six dependent variables including manipulation and likelihood of bank-proposed use.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the reputational risk the brief flags: whether an opt-out/default design in a bank app reads as helpful or manipulative, and shows savings-framed, transparent, deliberative defaults are best received — evidence for how to frame the entry decision, not just whether to default.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not real enrollment behavior
no measure of persistence or actual amounts saved
Australian sample, not EU
relevance_reason: Directly addresses consumer perception of financial defaults as manipulative vs. helpful, the EU dark-pattern reputational concern named in the brief.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries the choice of receiving transfers into bank accounts (vs. cash) had no significant average effect on savings, but raised balances for those with no prior savings.
methodology: Field experiment with conditional-cash-transfer beneficiaries in a developing-country context comparing cash vs. bank-account delivery.
why_it_matters: Tangential background on account-based saving mechanisms for low-savings populations, but not about enrollment defaults or round-up multipliers.
limitations: subsidy delivery choice, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrollment design
developing-country CCT population, not EU consumer banking app users
no measure of default vs. active enrollment
relevance_reason: Adjacent evidence on account-based saving uptake among low-balance individuals, weak fit to the enrollment-default question.

key_finding: The abstract fragment only notes that contribution amounts and program benefits on liquid funds are identical across compared cases; no effect size or design comparison is given.
methodology: abstract-only; details of study design not recoverable from the provided text.
why_it_matters: Too little information to inform any specific design decision; possibly relevant to emergency/liquid savings framing but unusable as presented.
limitations: abstract is a fragment with no findings
employer/policy-level automatic IRA context, not a consumer app
no effect sizes or comparisons stated
relevance_reason: Nominally about automatic enrollment with liquid savings but too thin to extract usable evidence.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and most enrollees stuck to the default contribution rate and fund allocation even three years later.
methodology: Before/after administrative-data analysis of one large U.S. corporation's 401(k) plan following a switch to automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that defaults both raise enrollment and anchor the contribution level — exactly the anchoring risk the brief asks about for the round-up multiplier — but in an employer-plan setting the brief says doesn't transfer directly.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), not a self-directed consumer app
single firm, single natural experiment
no comparison to active choice
relevance_reason: Foundational default/anchoring evidence the field argues with, capped for employer-plan setting.

key_finding: No abstract available; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviors between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined-contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only, unknown design.
why_it_matters: Potentially another auto- vs voluntary-enrollment comparison but no extractable findings to weigh against existing evidence.
limitations: no abstract text, findings unknown
employer-sponsored retirement plan setting
cannot assess effect size or persistence
relevance_reason: Topically on-point (auto vs voluntary enrollment) but unusable without abstract content.

key_finding: Low institutional trust and minority/non-national status are significantly associated with both under-saving and early withdrawal from a pension scheme following a policy reform allowing early access.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension early-withdrawal policy reform.
why_it_matters: Speaks to the brief's distributional concern (who is helped/hurt) and to the support team's worry about withdrawal, showing trust and demographic heterogeneity drive both under-saving and early withdrawal — relevant to designing safeguards, though in a mandatory pension context.
limitations: mandatory pension savings scheme, not a liquid consumer round-up product
correlational survey design
Estonian policy-specific context
relevance_reason: Distributional evidence on who under-saves and withdraws early, informing which users a default might harm.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrollment nudge policy reduced stated behavioral intentions and policy approval rather than increasing them.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a default (opt-out) nudge policy for vaccination.
why_it_matters: Shows that surfacing a default's mechanism can backfire on approval and intentions, a cautionary signal for how transparently the round-up default is communicated, though evidenced in a health rather than financial-product setting.
limitations: vaccination policy context, not financial/consumer product
hypothetical intentions, not observed behavior
no financial enrollment or amount data
relevance_reason: Contradicts an implicit assumption that defaults are uniformly well-received once made salient, relevant to manipulation-perception risk.

key_finding: Among Millennials, automatic enrollment and employer matching are associated with higher retirement-plan participation, while their absence is linked to non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study survey.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the well-established default effect on participation but adds little beyond existing employer-plan literature and does not touch persistence, amount, or active choice.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not self-directed consumer product
correlational survey data
no persistence or amount-saved measure
relevance_reason: Another confirmatory employer-plan enrollment study, largely redundant with stronger evidence already in the set.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic employer contributions (passive) raised total savings substantially, while subsidies requiring active choice mostly just shifted assets between accounts, with each $1 of subsidy raising saving by only 1 cent; 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish retirement savings policies distinguishing active vs. passive-choice mechanisms.
why_it_matters: The strongest existing evidence that passive/default mechanisms move actual saved amounts while active-choice incentives mostly relabel existing savings — central to the brief's question of whether defaults change nominal enrollment vs. real amounts saved, though in a retirement/tax-subsidy setting rather than liquid consumer savings.
limitations: government retirement-account subsidy setting, not a consumer app
no employer-app analogy stated for round-up feature
does not address the round-up multiplier anchoring question
relevance_reason: Landmark large-sample evidence on passive vs. active mechanisms changing real savings amounts, capped for retirement-policy setting.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision, no default) and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option are effective alternatives to automatic enrollment for motivating behavior change.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against opt-out/no-default conditions, reviewing prior automatic-enrollment savings applications.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the entry-design decision by testing the exact 'active choice' alternative the brief is weighing against opt-in/opt-out, including a specific enhanced variant that could recover most of the enrollment benefit of a default without full passive enrollment.
limitations: primary field tests are in medication adherence, not financial products
does not report persistence at 6-12 months for savings behavior specifically
no amount-saved outcome
relevance_reason: The originating study and only source directly comparing active choice/enhanced active choice against defaults, the mechanism the brief names as decision 1's third option.

key_finding: This NBER review synthesizes household-finance behavior and the choice-architecture interventions (defaults, product design, disclosure) that firms and governments use to shape financial outcomes, drawing on the behavioral economics literature on consumption and saving.
methodology: Narrative review/book chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and intervention evidence in household finance.
why_it_matters: Provides the synthesis-level view the brief asks for (a review giving effect-size context) across consumer financial behavior broadly, useful for calibrating how much weight to put on any single default study and where our round-up decision sits in the wider choice-architecture toolkit.
limitations: broad narrative review, not systematic protocol
not specific to fintech round-up products
authored by the same team behind the classic 401(k) default studies, so may overweight retirement-plan evidence
relevance_reason: Serves as the review/meta-level synthesis the brief explicitly wants alongside single-study estimates.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default fund, with half still doing so after three years, roughly offsetting the participation gain's effect on wealth accumulation on average.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms analyzing automatic enrollment effects on participation, default anchoring, and asset accumulation.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors long-run contribution choices, a direct warning for the round-up multiplier decision, though the mechanism is documented in an employer-plan setting the brief says doesn't transfer cleanly.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) plans, not a self-directed consumer app
three-firm sample
default rate anchoring shown for retirement contributions, not round-up multipliers
relevance_reason: Foundational quantitative evidence on default anchoring and its offsetting effect on real accumulation, capped for setting.

key_finding: In a randomized experiment on salary-linked savings accounts in Afghanistan, default enrollment increased participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% matching incentive — driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and it also shifted attitudes toward saving.
methodology: Randomized field experiment assigning employees to different default/enrollment varieties of a salary-linked savings account, with follow-up interventions isolating mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, causally identified effect size for the default effect on enrollment and, crucially, explains the mechanism (present bias, cognitive cost) — informing whether the lift from an opt-out design in our app is likely to be real behavior change or mere inertia, and whether it persists in attitudes afterward.
limitations: salary-linked account for employees, not a self-directed mobile banking app
developing-country context, different regulatory and liquidity environment
no long-run (6-12 month) withdrawal or amount-saved data reported
relevance_reason: Rare experimental evidence quantifying the default effect size and its causal mechanism, directly bearing on whether enrollment gains are genuine engagement or inertia.

key_finding: Payment reminders in a Brazilian financial-management app cut credit card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a consumer financial management platform, Brazil; fee outcomes tracked across credit card and checking accounts.
why_it_matters: Provides a concrete, quantified example of exactly the distributional risk the brief flags — a nudge that helps most users but harms a vulnerable subgroup — which should push the team toward measuring heterogeneous outcomes (not just aggregate enrolment) before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies reminder nudges, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
credit/overdraft fee context, not savings sign-up or savings amount
Brazilian consumer credit market, not EU round-up savings
relevance_reason: Directly evidences C5 (distributional/manipulation risk) with real effect sizes in a self-directed consumer fintech setting, supporting the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' concern even though it addresses a different nudge mechanism than enrolment defaults.
